Sure. Two years ago I owned the migration of our billing pipeline off a legacy cron system that was causing about $40k a month in mischarged invoices. I proposed the project after I traced three customer escalations to race conditions in the cron jobs. I was the sole backend engineer on it: I designed an event-driven architecture on SQS, wrote the reconciliation service, and led the cutover plan. We ran old and new systems in shadow mode for six weeks; I built the diff tooling that compared every invoice. At cutover, mischarge rate went from 0.7% of invoices to under 0.01%, and the on-call pages for billing dropped from about twelve a month to one.

The hardest part was that shadow mode kept surfacing diffs that weren't bugs in my system — they were bugs in the legacy system we were replacing. I had to decide whether to replicate the legacy behavior or fix it, invoice by invoice category. I wrote a one-page policy doc: replicate anything customer-visible unless it was overcharging, fix silently anything undercharging us, and flag overcharges to finance for refunds. Finance ended up refunding about $180k, which was uncomfortable to surface, but my director later said the proactive refund saved us in two enterprise renewals.

If I hadn't driven it, honestly, the migration was on the roadmap for 'next year' for three years running. The forcing function was the escalation analysis I did — once I put a dollar figure on the mischarges, it got prioritized in one planning cycle.

Yes — with our staff engineer, about whether the reconciliation service should be part of the billing monolith or standalone. He wanted it in the monolith: one deploy unit, shared models, no new infra to own. His strongest point was that our team had a bad track record operating extra services — we'd already had two orphaned microservices. I wanted it standalone because reconciliation needed to read from both old and new systems during migration, and coupling it to the monolith's deploy cycle would slow the shadow period. I proposed a compromise: standalone during migration, with a committed date to fold it into the monolith after cutover. We wrote down the criteria that would trigger the fold-in. He agreed, and we actually did fold it in four months after cutover — I did that work myself so it wouldn't become another orphan.

What I conceded was real: he was right about our operational track record, so I took his concern as a constraint rather than an objection. The written fold-in criteria were his idea originally and I adopted them. The relationship got stronger — he sponsored my promo case the next cycle and cited that decision doc specifically.

About eight months in, I shipped a change to the proration logic that undercharged annual-plan customers who upgraded mid-cycle. It passed review and tests because our test fixtures only covered monthly plans. A finance analyst caught it during month-end close, eighteen days after release — about $30k undercharged across 400 customers. The day it was found, I wrote the incident doc myself, quantified the exposure, and gave finance a per-customer breakdown within 24 hours so they could decide on collection versus write-off; they wrote it off. The root cause was mine: I'd assumed the fixtures were representative instead of checking coverage against real plan distribution. I added property-based tests that generate plan configurations from production distributions, and I changed our definition of done for billing changes to require a fixture-coverage check. Six months later a teammate's change tripped that same check before merge — that's the part I'm actually proud of.

The write-off decision wasn't mine, but I influenced it: collection would have cost more in support time and goodwill than the $30k. I laid out both options with estimated support load, and the VP of finance picked write-off in one meeting instead of the usual weeks of back-and-forth.

What changed in my behavior: before that incident I treated passing tests as sufficient evidence. Since then, for any money-touching change, I check what the test data actually covers against production reality first. It caught two more gaps in fixtures I would have shipped on top of previously.
